Aligning MLLMs with the Latent Structure of Human Cognition via Behavior-Derived Semantic Dimensions

Ning E ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: School of Biomedical Engineering, ShanghaiTech University, Shanghai, China Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China    Changde Du11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Affiliation: Zhongguancun Academy, Beijing, China    Yizhuo Lu11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Affiliation: School of Future Technology, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China    Huiguang He ††thanks: Corresponding author: huiguang.he@ia.ac.cn. Affiliation: School of Biomedical Engineering, ShanghaiTech University, Shanghai, China Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Affiliation: School of Future Technology, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Affiliation: Zhongguancun Academy, Beijing, China
Abstract

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. We build on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out (O1O) judgements. For each triplet, we infer the most salient decision dimension and convert it into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. This enables MLLMs to learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with the inferred behavioral criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves model consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Furthermore, using searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we observe increased representational alignment between model and human. Ultimately, our findings point to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLMs alignment. The code is available here.

1 Introduction

The advent of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) marks a major milestone in artificial intelligence, demonstrating strong performance across a spectrum of cognitive and reasoning tasks (Qwen Team, 2026; Bai et al., 2025a; Zeng et al., 2026) and naturally emerging human-like representations (Du et al., 2025). Current alignment paradigms (Fu et al., 2023; Sundaram et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2022; Schulman et al., 2017; Rafailov et al., 2023) focus on outcome-level behavioral mimicry, optimizing models to generate outputs that match human preferences without deeper human cognitive logic. Relying on this shallow mimicry leaves it unclear whether models solve tasks using human-consistent decision criteria or by exploiting statistical shortcuts. To realize more robust generalization, intrinsic interpretability, and authentic anthropomorphism, MLLMs alignment requires moving beyond behavioral mimicry toward the latent structure of human cognition.

To probe this alignment gap, we utilize the Odd-One-Out (O1O) task, a cornerstone of cognitive psychology for evaluating conceptual representations and reasoning. In this task, a subject is presented with three objects and must identify the one that is least similar to the other two. Identifying the odd object requires accessing the latent semantic dimensions that humans use to structure their conceptual world. Evaluating MLLMs on this task demonstrates that, despite their robust general capabilities, a persistent performance gap remains in predicting human choices. This disparity reveals a misalignment: standard approaches primarily align models with raw behavioral outcomes (i.e., what humans choose), failing to capture the underlying human cognition that dictates the decision criteria (i.e., why they choose it).

Our key insight to bridge this gap is to transform the latent structure of human cognition into explicit and learnable supervision. To achieve this, we build on the previous work of Hebart et al. (Hebart et al., 2020; Hebart et al., 2023), which established behavior-derived semantic embedding space. By analyzing 4.70 million human O1O judgements, they reveal interpretable 66-dimensional mental representations of natural objects underlying human similarity judgements. We adopt the 66-dimensional mental representations as the latent structure of human cognition to align MLLMs, enabling MLLMs to learn not only what humans choose, but also why they make choice. Concretely, for each triplet, we identify the most influential dimension driving human decision-making via the Jackknife (Mahner et al., 2025) method. However, a discrete semantic dimension is insufficient to bridge the gap with generative modality of MLLMs. To address this, we convert the discrete dimension into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale, which serves as an explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) constraint.

Building on this formulation, we construct the alignment dataset to fine-tune MLLMs, thereby deeply aligning their reasoning processes with the latent structure of human cognition. This is the concrete implementation of our framework. To validate the efficacy of our framework, we evaluate our framework along multiple axes. Behaviorally, the aligned MLLMs improve consistency with human similarity judgements compared to baselines, and retain competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Beyond behavioral aspect, we conduct searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008) using the independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) (Allen et al., 2022). The RSA results suggest that the internal representations of our aligned MLLMs demonstrate improved representational similarity to human neural activity. These neural results are not to reveal biological localization, but as a convergent, independent measure of similarity. Our findings demonstrate that explicitly incorporating behavior-derived cognitive priors is an effective and viable pathway for advancing the representational alignment between MLLMs and human cognitive structure.

Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We propose a novel alignment framework that moves beyond shallow behavioral mimicry by explicitly internalizing the latent structure of human cognition. By converting behavior-derived semantic dimensions into dimension-grounded linguistic rationales, MLLMs learn human-like decision-making cognition. (2) We introduce a pathway to integrate multidimensional mental representations from cognitive science into MLLMs. (3) Guided by this framework, we construct the alignment dataset that augments human similarity judgements with explicit rationales.

2 Related Work

Recent advances have made significant strides in aligning models with human cognitive behavior. Muttenthaler et al. improve neural network representations using human similarity judgements (Muttenthaler et al., 2023b) and find that model scale and architecture have essentially no effect on the alignment with human behavioral responses, whereas the training dataset and objective function both have a much larger impact (Muttenthaler et al., 2023a). AligNet (Muttenthaler et al., 2025) distills human similarity judgements from the THINGS dataset (Hebart et al., 2023) into vision models, successfully embedding human-like conceptual hierarchies into visual representations. In the video domain, Garcia and Isik (Garcia and Isik, 2026) introduce behavioral geometric supervision to align video representations with human judgements of social similarity, improving their correspondence with human social perception. Similarly, in the domain of Large Language Models (LLMs), Centaur (Binz et al., 2025) fine-tunes LLMs on an unprecedented scale of human behavioral data (Psych-101), demonstrating remarkable capabilities in predicting and simulating human behavior in any experiment expressible in natural language.

While these pioneering works establish the viability of using human behavioral data for model alignment, they primarily operate under the paradigm of outcome-level behavioral mimicry. By optimizing models directly toward human decision outcomes, these approaches implicitly assume that matching the output distribution entails capturing the underlying cognitive process. However, this leaves a critical gap: it remains opaque whether the models genuinely internalize the latent cognitive structure driving these decisions.

Our work builds on the foundation laid by these efforts but takes a step forward. Rather than relying on outcome matching, we argue that cognitive alignment in MLLMs requires explicit supervision of the reasoning process. By leveraging established behavior-derived semantic dimensions to construct dimension-grounded linguistic rationales, our framework explicitly models why a choice is made. This transforms the implicit cognitive structure into learnable CoT constraints, advancing the alignment paradigm from shallow behavioral mimicry to the integration of latent human cognitive structure.

3 Method

3.1 Triplet-Level Semantic Dimension Attribution

As illustrated in Figure 1, we first build on the established behavior-derived semantic embedding space introduced by Hebart et al. (Hebart et al., 2020; Hebart et al., 2023), specifically adopting the object-level semantic dimensions estimated via the Sparse Positive Similarity Embedding (SPoSE) (Zheng et al., 2019) model. To bridge these object representations with each triplet decision, we adopt a Jackknife-based attribution method to identify the most influential dimension underlying human similarity judgement.

Object embedding space.

As stated in the preliminaries A, given triplet objects 𝒯={i,j,k}\mathcal{T}=\{i,j,k\} (kk is odd-one-out), we define the probability that any two objects {u,v}⊂𝒯\{u,v\}\subset\mathcal{T} are identified as the most similar pair as p⁡(Wu,Wv)p(W_{u},W_{v}). This probability is computed via a softmax over the inner products of their embeddings WuW_{u} and WvW_{v}.

Triplet-level dimensions jackknife.

To infer which specific semantic dimension d∗d^{*} primarily drives a human decision (top-1 dimension), we employ a dimension Jackknife method. We iteratively ablate individual dimensions from the triplet objects embeddings. Let W^\hat{W} be the embedding vector where the dd dimension is pruned. We then recompute the ablated choice probability, denoted as p⁡(W^u,W^v)p(\hat{W}_{u},\hat{W}_{v}). The relevance score of dimension dd to the human judgement is quantified by the absolute probability difference:

Δp=|p⁡(Wi,Wj)−p⁡(W^i,W^j)|\Delta_{p}=\left|p(W_{i},W_{j})-p(\hat{W}_{i},\hat{W}_{j})\right| (1)

A larger Δp\Delta_{p} indicates that the original human choice is more sensitive to that pruned dimension. This process is repeated for all n=66n=66 dimensions to yield a relevance scores vector R1​…​66R_{1\dots 66}.

3.2 Dimension-Guided Reasoning Enhancement

While the Jackknife attribution effectively isolates the most influential semantic dimension d∗d^{*} driving human decision-making, utilizing discrete semantic labels (e.g., metallic or artificial) provides a sparse and contextually limited supervision signal. To address this, we convert the discrete semantic dimension d∗d^{*} label into an explicit, dimension-guided linguistic rationale r⁡(d∗)r(d^{*}) leveraging the generation capabilities of LLM.

As shown in Figure 2, for one triplet 𝒯\mathcal{T} and corresponding textual descriptions c​a​p​(𝒯)cap(\mathcal{T}), we synthesize the structured prompt 13, P​r​o​m​p​t​(𝒯,c​a​p​(𝒯),d∗)Prompt(\mathcal{T},cap(\mathcal{T}),d^{*}). Crucially, the LLM is not tasked with predicting the human choice. Instead, it is utilized exclusively as a reasoning enhancement engine. By injecting the semantic dimension d∗d^{*} into the prompt context, we guide the LLM to articulate exactly how this dimension drives human thinking and decision-making. The LLM processes the prompt to synthesize a coherent CoT reasoning path r⁡(d∗)r(d^{*}). Ultimately, these dimension-guided rationales provide high-quality, cognitively aligned supervisory data for the MLLMs alignment.

3.3 Cognitive Latent Structure Alignment

The final stage of our framework is to align MLLMs via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) using the derived explicit linguistic rationale r⁡(d∗)r(d^{*}). Current alignment paradigms predominantly rely on outcome-level supervision, optimizing models for behavioral mimicry without internalizing the underlying latent structure of human cognition. By explicitly anchoring the MLLMs in human-guided reasoning trajectories, we steer their internal decision-making mechanisms to align with the latent structure of human cognition.

Alignment optimization objective.

Given the visual input of triplet objects vv and the text instruction xinstx_{\text{inst}}, the enhanced reasoning trajectory is denoted as τ=[r⁡(d∗);y]\tau=[r(d^{*});y]. This formulation naturally factorizes the generative probability into two sequential cognitive phases: rationale generation (thinking) and final decision-making. Let θ\theta parameterize the MLLMs; the alignment objective over our dataset 𝒟O1O\mathcal{D}_{\text{O1O}} is formulated as:

ℒO1O​(θ)=−𝔼(𝐯,xinst,τ)∈𝒟O1O​[∑t=1τrlog⁡Pθ​(rt∣𝐯,xinst,r<t)+∑j=τr+1τr+τylog⁡Pθ​(yj∣𝐯,xinst,τr,y<j)]\mathcal{L}_{\text{O1O}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{v},x_{\text{inst}},\tau)\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{O1O}}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{\tau_{r}}\log P_{\theta}(r_{t}\mid\mathbf{v},x_{\text{inst}},r_{<t})+\sum_{j=\tau_{r}+1}^{\tau_{r}+\tau_{y}}\log P_{\theta}(y_{j}\mid\mathbf{v},x_{\text{inst}},\tau_{r},y_{<j})\right] (2)

where Pθ​(⋅)P_{\theta}(\cdot) denotes the autoregressive next-token prediction probability parameterized by the MLLMs. In this formulation, τr\tau_{r} and τy\tau_{y} denote the sequence lengths of the rationale and the final decision-making, respectively. During the initial reasoning phase (t∈[1,τr]t\in[1,\tau_{r}]), rtr_{t} represents the tt-th rationale token generated conditioned on the visual inputs 𝐯\mathbf{v}, the text instruction xinstx_{\text{inst}}, and the preceding tokens r<tr_{<t}. In the subsequent decision-making phase (j∈[τr+1,τr+τy]j\in[\tau_{r}+1,\tau_{r}+\tau_{y}]), yjy_{j} denotes the jj-th target token. Crucially, this second phase is conditioned on τr\tau_{r}, which herein represents the fully generated rationale sequence acting as a cognitive anchor. By optimizing this negative log-likelihood, we constrain the MLLMs internal decision-making mechanisms to internalize the latent human-like structure before the final decision.

Joint optimization.

While ℒO1O​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{O1O}}(\theta) effectively instills cognitive latent structure, fine-tuning exclusively on a narrow task distribution risks Catastrophic Forgetting (CF). To preserve foundational capabilities while aligning, we employ a joint optimization strategy. We use multi-task objective by mixing 𝒟O1O\mathcal{D}_{\text{O1O}} with a general-domain dataset 𝒟gen\mathcal{D}_{\text{gen}} (e.g., visual question answering data):

ℒ⁡(θ)=ℒO1O​(θ)+λ​ℒgen​(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\text{O1O}}(\theta)+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\text{gen}}(\theta) (3)

where ℒgen​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{gen}}(\theta) denotes the standard autoregressive next-token prediction loss on general multimodal data, ensuring the model retains its foundational generative capabilities. λ\lambda is a regularization hyperparameter, implemented via dynamic data sampling ratios during training (see Appendix G.4 for details). This multi-objective formulation allows the MLLMs to internalize human-consistent reasoning while retaining their broad generalization.

3.4 Neural Searchlight RSA

To provide a convergent, independent measure of representational alignment beyond behavioral evaluations, we conduct searchlight RSA using NSD. This neural evaluation is not intended to claim precise biological localization of MLLMs features, but rather to serve as a robust, modality-independent validation of our alignment framework. Given the same visual stimuli 𝒮\mathcal{S} for both MLLMs and human, we denote this as 𝒮={s1,s2​…,sn}\mathcal{S}=\{s_{1},s_{2}\dots,s_{n}\} and compute Representational Dissimilarity Matrix (RDM).

MLLMs RDM.

After extracting the internal representations via a forward propagation (detailed in Appendix F.1), we denote hi∈ℝDh_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} as the DD-dimensional hidden state vector extracted from the <|vision_end|> token for sis_{i}. We quantify the internal representational geometry by computing the MLLMs RDM, denoted as R​D​MM∈ℝS×SRDM^{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times S}. The pairwise representational dissimilarity between any two stimuli sis_{i} and sjs_{j} is defined as:

R​D​Mi,jM=1−ρ⁡(hi,hj)RDM^{M}_{i,j}=1-\rho(h_{i},h_{j}) (4)

where ρ⁡(⋅,⋅)\rho(\cdot,\cdot) is the Pearson correlation coefficient across the DD feature dimensions.

Human RDM.

For a spherical searchlight neighborhood centered at voxel cc comprising CC contiguous voxels (radius = 3 voxels), let bic∈ℝCb_{i}^{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} denote the local multi-voxel neural activation pattern elicited by stimulus sis_{i}. The corresponding localized RDM, denoted as R​D​Mc∈ℝS×SRDM^{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times S}, is computed by:

R​D​Mi,jc=1−ρ⁡(bic,bjc)RDM^{c}_{i,j}=1-\rho(b_{i}^{c},b_{j}^{c}) (5)

Searchlight RSA score.

To quantify the representational alignment between the MLLMs internal representation space and the localized human cortex, we compute the voxel-wise neural alignment score, R​S​A​(ℳ,c)RSA(\mathcal{M},c). Let u⁡(⋅)u(\cdot) denote the operator that extracts the flattened upper triangular elements of a given RDM, excluding the main diagonal. The alignment score at searchlight center cc is defined as the Spearman correlation coefficient between the respective upper triangular vectors:

R​S​A​(ℳ,c)=ρs​(u⁡(R​D​MM),u⁡(R​D​Mc))RSA(\mathcal{M},c)=\rho_{s}(u(RDM^{M}),u(RDM^{c})) (6)

To evaluate the representational enhancement driven by our alignment framework, we compute the voxel-wise alignment shift, denoted as ΔR​S​A​(c)\Delta_{RSA}(c). This shift quantifies the difference in alignment scores between the aligned MLLMs (ℳa​l​i​g​n\mathcal{M}_{align}) and the unaligned baseline (ℳb​a​s​e\mathcal{M}_{base}):

ΔR​S​A​(c)=R​S​A​(ℳa​l​i​g​n,c)−R​S​A​(ℳb​a​s​e,c)\Delta_{RSA}(c)=RSA(\mathcal{M}_{align},c)-RSA(\mathcal{M}_{base},c) (7)

Prior to cortical projection, we apply a lower-bound threshold to the alignment shift map to filter out negligible negative fluctuations. Empirically, negative ΔR​S​A​(c)\Delta_{RSA}(c) values are extremely close to zero and arise from computational noise rather than meaningful representational degradation. Therefore, we clamp these values to a near-zero floor (ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}):

Δ~R​S​A​(c)=max⁡(ϵ,ΔR​S​A​(c))\tilde{\Delta}_{RSA}(c)=\max(\epsilon,\Delta_{RSA}(c)) (8)

The resulting non-negative alignment shift map, Δ~R​S​A\tilde{\Delta}_{RSA}, is then projected onto a flattened cortical surface using pycortex (Gao et al., 2015).

4 Experiments

4.1 Dataset

We construct a hybrid dataset including 𝒟O1O\mathcal{D}_{\text{O1O}} and 𝒟gen\mathcal{D}_{\text{gen}}. The composition is summarized in Figure 3 (a) and examples are shown in Figure 3 (b). Details are provided in Appendix G.

4.2 Setup

We conduct experiments across the Qwen3-VL (Bai et al., 2025a) model family, specifically utilizing the ∼\sim4B and ∼\sim8B instruction models, as well as the ∼\sim30B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model. We denote the aligned models fine-tuned via our framework as CogAlign, and their unaligned counterparts as Baseline. Full implementation details are provided in Appendix H.1.

In addition to these MLLMs, we incorporate Centaur, a foundation model of human cognition. This serves as a specialized external reference, allowing us to benchmark our aligned models against an architecture optimized for cognitive tasks.

4.3 Main Result

Generalization performance.

A critical concern in model alignment is the potential degradation of general capabilities. To investigate whether aligning with the latent structures of human cognition compromises broader reasoning abilities, we evaluate both the baseline and aligned models on two multimodal benchmarks: MMMU (Yue et al., 2024) (val) and MMBench (Liu et al., 2024) (en, test).

As reported in Table 1, we evaluate the general capabilities to investigate the potential alignment tax. The results indicate a trade-off: while the aligned models achieve consistent performance gains across all scales on MMMUval\text{MMMU}_{\text{val}} benchmark (e.g., +4.34 improvement for Qwen3-VL-30B), they exhibit a minor degradation on MMBenchen, test\text{MMBench}_{\text{en, test}} compared to their unaligned baselines. This suggests that aligning with human cognitive latent structure incurs a slight alignment tax on general-purpose multimodal tasks.

Human consistency.

We quantify human consistency using accuracy on the O1O validation set comprising 453,642 held-out triplets, where higher accuracy indicates better alignment. This massive scale ensures that our evaluation captures robust results rather than anecdotal success.

As detailed in Table 2, we evaluate the models against two distinct baseline settings to establish a comprehensive comparison. In the Direct prompt 15 setting, the model is prompted to output the final option (e.g., A, B, or C) immediately. In the CoT prompt 16 setting, the model is required to think step-by-step before decision-making. The results demonstrate that our alignment framework yields improvements over both baseline settings and the performance of aligned models remains stable across all scales (ranging from 56.2156.21 to 56.9956.99). While the aligned models outperform not only the Direct baselines but also more capable CoT baselines across all models, the relative gain over the CoT baseline narrows as model capacity increases. This shrinking delta is due to the upward trajectory of the baseline itself.

To rigorously validate these gains, we report 95% Confidence Intervals (CIs) estimated via bootstrap resampling. For the Qwen3-VL series, the CIs of the aligned models (e.g., [56.70,57.28][56.70,57.28] for the ∼\sim8B model) do not overlap with those of their respective baselines, indicating a statistically significant enhancement in human-model consistency by a McNemar test (McNemar, 1947) (p<0.001p<0.001).

Neuroscientific analysis.

To investigate whether our framework improves the alignment between the internal representational geometry of MLLMs and the human brain, we analyze the neural alignment shift (Δ~R​S​A​(c)\tilde{\Delta}_{RSA}(c)). Following the method detailed in Section 3.4, this shift is computed using the concatenated hidden states from the MLLMs last four layers and visualized via cortical projection.

As illustrated in Figures 4 and 5, the resulting cortical heatmaps reveal consistent representational alignment improvements across all subjects (subject 1, 2, 5, and 7 (Takagi and Nishimoto, 2023; Scotti et al., 2023); paired t-test, p<0.001p<0.001). Detailed discussion of these results is provided in the Appendix H.6.

4.4 Ablation Result

Necessity of alignment over prompting.

To determine whether MLLMs can show human-like cognitive structures purely via inference-time prompting or if our alignment is necessary, we ablate the Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct baseline against three prompting strategies: (1) Standard CoT (S-CoT 16), which uses unconstrained step-by-step reasoning. (2) d∗d^{*}-Guided CoT (d∗d^{*}-CoT 17), which strictly constrains reasoning to the most salient semantic dimension (d∗d^{*}). (3) Full-Space CoT (FS-CoT 18), which requires dynamic grounding one or more dimension(s) across the complete 66-dimensional behavioral semantic space.

As shown in Table 3, we compare inference-time prompting with our alignment framework on Qwen3-VL Instruct model. Although explicitly providing semantic dimensions enables the model to access these concepts during reasoning, it does not guarantee stable reasoning over these dimensions. Neither d∗d^{*}-CoT nor FS-CoT consistently improves over standard reasoning (S-CoT). d∗d^{*}-CoT reduces performance from 53.37 to 49.01, suggesting that imposing a cognitive dimension may constrain the model’s decision process without ensuring effective utilization of the underlying semantic information. Similarly, FS-CoT achieves 52.70, remaining comparable to S-CoT. In contrast, our CogAlign achieves 56.8156.81, exceeding S-CoT and FS-CoT by 3.443.44 and 4.114.11 percentage points, respectively. Our framework incorporates these latent cognitive structures into the model, enabling more consistent human-like decision patterns.

Generalizability across MLLMs families.

To verify that our alignment framework is architecture-agnostic, we extend our evaluation to Qwen2.5-VL (Bai et al., 2025b) and Gemma3 (Kamath et al., 2025) instruction models. To balance computational efficiency with reliability, we conduct this ablation on a subset (∼\sim75.6K triplets, 1/6) of the O1O validation set.

As reported in Table 4, our framework yields consistent improvements in human behavioral consistency across distinct model families. The aligned Qwen2.5-VL and Gemma3 outperform their respective CoT baselines by 2.66 and 1.51.

Similarity of behavioral representational geometry.

Beyond agreement on triplet choices, we examine whether alignment captures the broader organization of human similarity judgements.

Choice-based representational similarity matrices (RSMs) represent pairwise similarity relationships among objects, allowing us to assess model-human correspondence at the level of behavioral representational geometry. We compute the Pearson correlation of the choice-based RSMs derived from Qwen2.5-VL-7B and human on a 48-object subset (∼\sim91.56K triplets) drawn from the complete dataset. As shown in Figure 6, the aligned model achieves 80.93% exceeding its CoT baseline 73.30% and Centaur 65.13%. These results suggest that alignment improves correspondence with human behavioral representational geometry beyond triplet choices. Details are provided in Appendix H.7.

5 Conclusion

In this paper, we present a data-driven framework to align MLLMs with the latent structure of human cognition via behavior-derived semantic dimensions. Moving beyond outcome-level mimicry, our framework translates the multidimensional mental representations of natural objects underlying human similarity judgements into explicit linguistic rationales, enabling MLLMs to internalize these priors. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of our alignment framework. The aligned MLLMs achieve improvements in behavioral consistency with human. Ablation studies reveal that these cognitive priors should be internalized: providing semantic dimensions via inference-time prompting paradoxically degrades performance, suggesting a fundamental gap between prompting and our framework. Furthermore, independent searchlight RSA indicates that the MLLMs internal representations become more aligned with human neural activity after aligning. While a minor trade-off is observed on general benchmarks, this work provides a proof-of-concept for bridging cognitive science and MLLMs alignment. Our framework points to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLMs alignment. We hope this work inspires further exploration toward developing more controllable, transparent, and human-like artificial cognitive systems. Furthermore, to clarify the commensurability of our baselines and explicitly outline the value of this process-level alignment framework for both the machine learning and cognitive science communities, we provide extended discussion in Appendix E.

6 Limitations

While our framework improves alignment between MLLMs and the latent structure of human cognition, we note some limitations.

Our triplet-level semantic dimension attribution relies on a top-1 approximation, identifying a single dominant dimension (d∗d^{*}). This isolates the primary semantic axis, but does not model the joint contributions of multiple dimensions or their context-dependent interactions. The resulting supervision may therefore simplify the structure underlying human similarity judgements.

The 66 behavior-derived semantic dimensions are object-centric, characterizing perceptual and conceptual properties primarily. Although this space includes some abstract dimensions, such as valuable or precious and weapon-related (Table 12), their presence does not establish coverage of the abstractions required for mathematical reasoning or reasoning about complex geometric and topological structures. Consequently, the applicability of our alignment framework to highly abstract multimodal domains remains to be further explored (see Appendix B for details).

As with many synthesized datasets, the rationales generated in our pipeline are not flawless. While our framework strictly grounds every rationale in a valid, human-derived cognitive dimension, the subsequent verbalization by the LLMs can occasionally introduce factual inconsistencies or ad hoc associations. We provide transparent and detailed discussion in Appendix C.

The improvement over the CoT baseline becomes smaller for larger models. This trend is driven by the emergent conceptual structures inherent in stronger models, which raises the initial untuned performance closer to our current alignment ceiling (see Appendix D for details).

Appendix A Preliminaries

Prior experimental, neuropsychological and neuroimaging evidence have led to the proposal of object dimensions such as animacy, manipulability and real-world size (Caramazza and Shelton, 1998; Chao et al., 1999; Konkle and Oliva, 2011), but these dimensions describe only a selective and largely incomplete portion of our mental representational space. Our work builds on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, which provides visual and conceptual mental representations for a wide, representative range of natural objects (Hebart et al., 2020; Hebart et al., 2023). Specifically, this space maps a set of 1854 object concepts into a sparse and non-negative vector space, where each dimension corresponds to a distinct conceptual and perceptual property (e.g., metallic, animal-related, textile).

A.1 Sparse Positive Similarity Embedding (SPoSE)

We introduce the SPoSE proposed by Charles Y. Zheng et al. (Zheng et al., 2019) in this section. SPoSE is based on three assumptions.

Semantic representation of concepts.

The first assumption is that each object concept cic_{i} can be represented by semantic features, quantified in a vector 𝐱𝐢=(xi​1,…,xi​p){\bf x_{i}}=(x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ip}). These features correspond dimensions of a latent space where the geometrical relationships encode conceptual (dis)similarity. The SPoSE model estimates these features from behavioral data alone using the probabilistic model. To ensure interpretability, the SPoSE model constrains each dimension xi​fx_{if} in the vector 𝐱𝐢{\bf x_{i}} to be real and non-negative, reflecting the degree to which the aspect of meaning it represents is present and influences subject behavior (Murphy et al., 2012). Furthermore, a sparsity constraint is added to the SPoSE model for sparse these dimensions (McRae et al., 2005).

Probabilistic model.

The second assumption is that the decision in a triplet task trial is explained by the similarity between the embedding vectors of the presented concepts. For any two concepts cic_{i} and cjc_{j}, the SPoSE model defines the similarity Si​jS_{ij} as the dot product of their corresponding vectors:

Si​j=⟨𝐱𝐢,𝐱𝐣⟩=∑f=1pxi​f​xj​f.S_{ij}=\langle{\bf x_{i}},{\bf x_{j}}\rangle=\sum_{f=1}^{p}x_{if}x_{jf}. (9)

The third assumption models the outcome of the triplet task as a stochastic process. This assumption reflects both trial-to-trial inconsistencies in how an individual subject makes the decision, as well as subject differences in the decision-making process. To account for behavioral inconsistencies, the probability of a subject choosing a specific pair is modeled by Softmax Action Selection:

Pr⁡[y1,y2]∝exp⁡(Sy1,y2)\Pr[y_{1},y_{2}]\propto\exp(S_{y_{1},y_{2}}) (10)

Since probabilities of the three possible outcomes add to one, this gives

Pr⁡[y1,y2]=exp⁡(Sy1,y2)exp⁡(Si1,i2)+exp⁡(Si1,i3)+exp⁡(Si2,i3)\Pr[y_{1},y_{2}]=\frac{\exp(S_{y_{1},y_{2}})}{\exp(S_{i_{1},i_{2}})+\exp(S_{i_{1},i_{3}})+\exp(S_{i_{2},i_{3}})} (11)

In this formulation, the vectors 𝐱𝐢{\bf x_{i}} are unnormalized. This design choice allows vector similarities to be arbitrarily large, modeling situations where decision is near-deterministic (e.g., when two concepts are virtually identical).

Parameter fitting.

The embedding vectors (𝐱𝟏,…,𝐱𝐦)({\bf x_{1}},\ldots,{\bf x_{m}}) are inferred by minimizing a regularized maximum likelihood objective function. For the given triplets datasets (total number is nn), where (i1,j,i2,j,i3,j)(i_{1,j},i_{2,j},i_{3,j}) denotes the concepts in the jj-th triplet and (y1,j,y2,j)(y_{1,j},y_{2,j}) indicates the chosen pair. The objective function to be minimized is defined as:

∑j=1nt​r​a​i​nlog⁡(exp⁡(𝐱𝐲𝟏,𝐣T​𝐱𝐲𝟐,𝐣)exp⁡(𝐱𝐢𝟏,𝐣T​𝐱𝐢𝟐,𝐣)+exp⁡(𝐱𝐢𝟏,𝐣T​𝐱𝐢𝟑,𝐣)+exp⁡(𝐱𝐢𝟐,𝐣T​𝐱𝐢𝟑,𝐣))+λ​∑i=1m‖𝐱𝐢‖1\sum_{j=1}^{n_{train}}\log\left(\frac{\exp({\bf x_{y_{1,j}}}^{T}{\bf x_{y_{2,j}}})}{\exp({\bf x_{i_{1,j}}}^{T}{\bf x_{i_{2,j}}})+\exp({\bf x_{i_{1,j}}}^{T}{\bf x_{i_{3,j}}})+\exp({\bf x_{i_{2,j}}}^{T}{\bf x_{i_{3,j}}})}\right)+\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{m}||{\bf x_{i}}||_{1} (12)

where pp is specified number of dimensions, nt​r​a​i​nn_{train} is the number of training triplets. ||⋅||1||\cdot||_{1} is the L1 norm, so ‖𝐱‖1=∑f=1p|xf|||{\bf x}||_{1}=\sum_{f=1}^{p}|x_{f}|, and xf≥0x_{f}\geq 0 for f=1,…,pf=1,\ldots,p. λ\lambda is the regularization parameter.

A.2 Behavior-Derived Embedding Space via SPoSE

The object representations are learned from human similarity judgement behavioral data using the SPoSE model. In the triplet O1O task, participants are presented with three objects, i,j,i,j, and kk, and asked to identify the most dissimilar one. Assuming kk is chosen as the odd-one-out, the psychological similarity between ii and jj is considered the highest among the pairs. SPoSE models this by assigning a non-negative latent vector 𝐱∈ℝ≥0d\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{d} to each object. The probability of choosing kk as the odd-one-out is formulated using a softmax over the inner products of the object vectors:

P⁡(k∣i,j,k)=exp⁡(𝐱i⊤​𝐱j)exp⁡(𝐱i⊤​𝐱j)+exp⁡(𝐱i⊤​𝐱k)+exp⁡(𝐱j⊤​𝐱k)P(k\mid i,j,k)=\frac{\exp(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{j})}{\exp(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{j})+\exp(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{k})+\exp(\mathbf{x}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{k})} (13)

By applying L1L_{1} regularization during optimization, SPoSE enforces sparsity and non-negativity, ensuring that the resulting dimensions are interpretable as the latent structure of human cognition (Hebart et al., 2020).

A.3 Justification for 66 Dimensions

The critical property of this embedding space is its dimensionality, d = 66. In many representation learning contexts, dimensionality is treated as an arbitrary hyperparameter tuned for downstream performance. However, in this behavior-derived space, d=66d=66 is saturation. Analysis conducted by Hebart et al. (Hebart et al., 2023) demonstrates that while the number of reproducible dimensions scales with the volume of behavioral data, it ultimately saturates around 67.5 dimensions and would reach ∼66.5\sim 66.5 dimensions for 4.5−54.5-5 million trials. Indeed, when re-running the SPoSE model with the full dataset of 4.70 million trials (4.10 million for training), embedding dimensionality turns out as predicted: from a set of 72 randomly-initialized models, they choose the most reliable embedding as the final embedding, revealing 66 interpretable dimensions underlying perceived similarity judgements. Thus, increasing dataset size beyond this large dataset may no longer yield noticeable improvements in predictive performance or changes in embedding dimensionality at the global level of similarity, and potential improvements may not justify the cost of collecting additional data. These 66 dimensions represent a data-driven, globally saturated approximation of the latent structure of human cognition used to conceptualize this broad set of natural objects. This provides a rigorous and interpretable foundation for our proposed alignment framework.

Appendix B Impact of Incorporating Abstract Dimensions

Our alignment framework makes no assumptions about the semantic content of the dimensions. Incorporating richer abstract dimensions therefore requires replacing or augmenting the embedding space rather than modifying the core framework.

We envision three pathways for this integration: (a) Swapping the behavioral substrate. Applying the identical pipeline to O1O data collected on stimuli where abstract criteria dominate (e.g., social or moral scenarios). (b) Augmenting the existing space. Concatenating normative ratings for objects along abstract attributes with the SPoSE dimensions before Jackknife attribution, allowing the attribution step to decide whether an abstract or object-centric criterion best explains the human choice. (c) Context-conditioned judgements. Since abstract criteria often become decision-relevant only under specific contexts, collecting context-conditioned O1O data and injecting this context into the rationale prompt.

Abstract criteria (e.g., social acceptability) are substantially more subject- and culture-dependent, introducing variability into the decision-making process. While this could enhance the model’s alignment with complex human values, it also raises the bias-auditing concerns we raise in the Impact Statement. As illustrated by the emergent stereotypical gender dimensions, behaviorally derived abstract axes can encode societal norms or biases that human may not wish to instill wholesale, necessitating careful curation when expanding the semantic space.

Appendix C Rationale Quality Analysis

In our framework, the supervision signal originates from two distinct sources. (1) Human Population: The decisive supervisory anchor, the choice and its operative cognitive dimension, is attributed from 4.70M validated human judgements via SPoSE and Jackknife. (2) LLM Generator: The LLM role is strictly restricted to verbalizing this behaviorally grounded criterion without altering the underlying decision.

A concern regarding this pipeline is the quality of the LLM-generated rationales. Since no generation is flawless, we conduct a transparent diagnostic of the rationale quality, evaluate the robustness of the framework across different rationale generators, and clarify why the framework yields robust gains despite data imperfections.

Independent MLLM-as-judge diagnostic.

To quantitatively evaluate rationale quality without self-preference bias, we employ a stronger, independent MLLM (Kimi-K3 (Bai et al., 2026)) as a rubric-based judge on a random sample of training rationales. Given the triplet images, the corresponding dimension, and the rationale, the judge scores four independent criteria:

  • •

    Dimension faithfulness (D): The given dimension is the actual operative basis of the comparison.

  • •

    Factual correctness (F): Claims about the objects are visually supported or represent stable common knowledge.

  • •

    Logical validity (L): The stated premises consistently entail the odd-one-out choice.

  • •

    Non-forcedness (N): The dimension-object relation is conventional and discriminative, penalizing ad hoc associations.

As shown in Table 5, for Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct generator, the independent MLLM-as-judge diagnostic reveals that while 93.37% of rationales are faithfully grounded in the assigned dimension, only about 70.45% are strictly logically valid, 73.11% are factually flawless, and 54.73% are completely non-forced. Despite these verbalization imperfections, our results confirm that the framework consistently improves alignment across multiple MLLMs and generator LLMs.

Cross-generator semantic convergence and robustness.

To ensure that the framework effectiveness does not rely on the idiosyncrasies of a single generator (Qwen2.5-72B (Yang et al., 2025)), we regenerate the full set rationales using DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026) under identical prompts.

Semantic convergence: Using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025b), we compute the pairwise semantic similarity between rationales produced by the two generators for identical triplets. The high similarity (Mean = 83.39%, Std = 5.93%) confirms that different LLMs converge on similar reasoning pathways when anchored by the same cognitive dimension.

Performance robustness: We fine-tune the Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct using the generated DeepSeek-V4-Flash rationales. The accuracy (56.52%) closely matches our original result using Qwen2.5-72B rationales (56.81%), and exceeds the CoT baseline (53.37%).

Why imperfect rationales drive consistent improvement.

A question arises: if a substantial proportion of training rationales are identified as flawed or forced, why should they be included, and why do they still drive performance improvements?

We argue that this highlights a core strength of our approach. The foundational anchor of every sample remains a valid human consensus. Even when the LLM verbalization is imperfect or slightly forced, it still forces the model to map its internal representations toward a validated human cognitive dimension rather than relying on uninterpretable statistical shortcuts. Crucially, our experiments demonstrate that the performance gains are the property of this dual-supervision framework. The exact same unfiltered dataset yields consistent improvements across five different MLLMs configurations spanning multiple scales and architectures (e.g., Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, Gemma3 in Tables 2 and 4). The fact that alignment gains replicate across multiple architectures and independent rationale generators, despite the quantified imperfections, provides strong evidence that the improvement stems from the structure of the framework itself rather than data curation.

While employing a closed-loop validation procedure or a frontier model (like Kimi-K3) to regenerate and filter the dataset would undoubtedly improve data quality and aligned model performance, such large-scale regeneration is often economically prohibitive for exploratory studies. Our findings confirm that even with accessible open-weight generators and inherently noisy verbalizations, injecting human cognitive priors explicitly via this framework improves alignment.

Appendix D Scaling Dynamics and Alignment Ceiling Analysis

As observed in our main results (Table 2), the relative accuracy gain of our aligned model over the CoT baseline diminishes as the parameter size of the MLLM increases. We decompose this scaling trend to provide more detailed discussion.

Across all model scales, the absolute performance of our aligned models remains remarkably stable: 56.81 (4B), 56.99 (8B), and 56.21 (30B). The shrinking delta is driven by the rising CoT baseline. Stronger MLLMs emerge human-like conceptual structures and world knowledge during large-scale pre-training. Consequently, the untuned starting point of larger models naturally moves closer to the human-like behavioral target, leaving less accessible headroom for our current alignment formulation. Currently, our pipeline only relies on top-1 dimension, supervising the model with a single dominant criterion. However, human similarity judgements are often nuanced, involving complex trade-offs among multiple cognitive dimensions. Supervising only the primary axis creates an implicit upper bound on task performance. Furthermore, our current alignment dataset comprises 80K sampled triplets, representing only ∼\sim2% of the 4.1M available training triplets.

This yields a concrete, testable prediction for future alignment research: enriching the supervision signal through multidimensional rationales and scaling the alignment data far beyond the current ∼\sim2% sample should effectively break the ceiling. As model capabilities increase, they possess the representational capacity to absorb these denser, multi-faceted cognitive priors.

Appendix E Framework Scope and Interdisciplinary Value

We further clarify the conceptual scope of our alignment framework, delineate its distinction from existing baselines, and outline its specific utility for researchers.

Baseline commensurability and process-level internalization.

A core contribution of our work is shifting the alignment pathway for MLLMs from outcome-level behavioral mimicry to the process-level internalization of latent human cognitive structures. This distinction determines which baselines are commensurable with our approach. Post-hoc feature reweighting and selection methods operate as readouts on frozen feature spaces, producing task-specific discriminative mappings. They do not modify the model’s internal reasoning and they are difficult to apply to the autoregressive generative setting of MLLMs. Consequently, the appropriate same-class baseline is a behaviorally fine-tuned model.

As reported in our main results, we compare against Centaur, which is fine-tuned on the largest existing human behavioral corpus (Psych-101). Our aligned models outperform Centaur both behaviorally and in representational similarity in Table 2 and Figure 6. Furthermore our prompting ablations in Table 3 function as a non-parametric analogue to feature selection. This demonstrates that cognitive criteria should be internalized through joint rationale-decision supervision, rather than merely provided as external features.

Broad use cases and value for researchers.

Beyond empirical performance, our framework offers a general, data-efficient recipe for injecting population-level cognitive priors into MLLMs without requiring architectural modifications.

For LLMs/MLLMs researchers, the primary value lies in intrinsic interpretability and controllability. Because every decision made by the model is preceded by a rationale grounded in an interpretable, behaviorally validated dimension, the decision processes become directly auditable against known human criteria. Moreover, the proposed framework is domain-agnostic. It enables researchers to convert existing large-scale cognitive science datasets into rich process-level supervision, facilitating the development of controllable, consensus-consistent LLMs/MLLMs.

For neuroscientists and cognitive scientists, the models additionally offer a new class of testable computational models and can be subjects for hypothesis generation about related tasks to reduce the difficulty and cost of data sampling. Our work also encourages relevant researchers to shift their focus from outcome-level studies to a deeper exploration of the underlying cognitive reasoning processes.

Appendix F Method Details

F.1 Internal Feature Extraction via Forward Propagation

To map the MLLMs internal representations to human brain activity, we construct a multimodal input using a neutral instruction prompt (Describe this image) alongside the visual stimuli and perform forward propagation pass through baseline and aligned MLLMs. Targeting the most representative feature, we extract the hidden states specifically from the <|vision_end|> token which is the special token delimiting the end of the visual embedding sequence for Qwen3-VL series models. We extract these states from three specific depths: the last layer, the second-to-last layer, and the last four layers (Devlin et al., 2019). We prioritize this token over individual spatial image pad tokens or subsequent text tokens for two fundamental reasons: (1) Global Visual Integration: Unlike individual image pad tokens which encode spatially localized features, the <|vision_end|> token serves as a global aggregator. Due to the causal attention mechanism of the LLM backbone, this token attends to the entire preceding visual sequence, effectively summarizing the holistic visual semantic content before text begins. (2) Vision-Language Boundary: This token represents the terminal state of visual perception and the initial state of text. It is the bottleneck where visual features are projected into the semantic manifold, making it the most theoretically plausible candidate for alignment with human cortical representations.

Appendix G Data Details

G.1 Statistics

Table 6 summarizes the composition of our hybrid training dataset, reporting sample counts and proportions for cognitive-alignment data and generalization data across single-image and multi-image tasks.

G.2 Cognitive-Alignment Data

O1O task data to align the latent structure of human cognition. 𝒟O1O\mathcal{D}_{\text{O1O}} is constructed via method 3.2 using prompt 14.

G.3 Generalization Data

We supplement 𝒟O1O\mathcal{D}_{\text{O1O}} with a diverse set of regularization data 𝒟gen\mathcal{D}_{\text{gen}} selected from open-source datasets, categorized into Single-image and multi-image scenarios:

Single-image scenarios.

We incorporate COCO (Lin et al., 2014), ALLaVA-4V (Chen et al., 2024), and LLaVAR (Zhang et al., 2024).

Multi-image scenarios.

Since the Odd-One-Out task inherently involves comparing multiple images (a triplet), we specifically include multi-image reasoning tasks from M4-Instruct (Li et al., 2025), such as Spot the Difference (Jhamtani and Berg-Kirkpatrick, 2018; Park et al., 2019), Image Edit Instruction (Zhang et al., 2023; Bodur et al., 2024), Visual Storytelling (Ravi et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2016), Text-rich VQA, and Low-level Comparison (Fu et al., 2023; Sundaram et al., 2024). This ensures that the model learns to process multi-image text sequences robustly, rather than overfitting to the specific three-image format of the O1O task.

G.4 Dynamic Stratified Data Sampling

Given the diverse nature of our training mixture (ranging from O1O cognitive data to general data), utilizing a naive data loader could lead to distributional shifts between batches (e.g., a batch dominated solely by one task type). To mitigate this, we implement a dynamic stratified sampling strategy.

Specifically, we define the sampling probability for each task kk based on its proportion in the total dataset. During training, for every global step, we construct the mini-batch by sampling data points from each task category proportional to these ratios, constrained by the total global batch size across all GPUs. The samples within each constructed batch are then shuffled using a fixed random seed.

This strategy guarantees that every gradient update vector is computed from a representative distribution of both cognitive alignment signals and general regularization data. By stabilizing the gradient direction and preventing task-specific bias during optimization, this sampling method is helpful for retaining the model’s generalization capabilities while effectively instilling the latent structure of human cognition.

Appendix H Experimental Details

We provide a comprehensive overview of our experimental setup, including the hyperparameters for Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).

H.1 Training Details

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

As shown in Table 8, the SFT stage utilizes AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) and a cosine learning rate scheduler with a peak learning rate of 1​e-​51\text{e-}5. We total use 6 ×\times NVIDIA A800 80G GPUs with TRL (von Werra et al., 2020), Qwen-VL utils (QwenLM, 2026), and DeepSpeed (Rajbhandari et al., 2020).

H.2 Evaluation Details

We conduct a comprehensive evaluation using the vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). For evaluation metrics, we adopt traditional exact string matching to accurately assess response correctness about human consistency. Following the guidelines from the official vLLM documentation, we set the temperature to 0.00.0, top-p to 1.01.0, and top-k to −1-1. We apply a repetition penalty of 1.051.05 and limit the maximum response length to 81928192 tokens.

To ensure a strictly fair comparison, we re-evaluate all baselines on our local infrastructure rather than relying on reported metrics. We observe a performance discrepancy between local reproduction and reported results, a known issue in benchmark evaluation (ArdalanM, 2025). Therefore, we report results for both the Baseline and our CogAlign models under the exact same experimental setting. Specifically, we employ the lmms-eval framework (Zhang et al., 2025a; Li* et al., 2024) and adhere strictly to its default parameters for MMMU and MMBench benchmarks. By using the standard default parameters, we eliminate potential biases arising from hyperparameter tuning.

H.3 Generalization Performance Details

Table 9 reports detailed results on the MMBench(en,test) for the baseline and CogAlign variants of Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen3-VL-8B, and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B. In addition to overall scores, it provides breakdowns by general capability and specific task, allowing a finer-grained comparison of performance before and after cognitive alignment.

H.4 Necessity of Alignment over Prompting

We use a more lenient parser for d∗d^{*}-CoT and FS-CoT settings because of their generation failures and manually examine the parsing failures. We find that almost all failures are not caused by minor formatting variations or an overly strict parser. Instead, the model frequently enters a highly repetitive generation loop, repeatedly enumerating irrelevant positive and negative attributes. Consequently, it exhausts the maximum generation length before producing the required closing tag. Thus, such cases represent genuine generation failures rather than correct predictions that are rejected solely because of formatting. We list an example of parsing failures below.

H.5 Necessity of Dimension-Grounded Rationales

To isolate the exact drivers of our framework alignment gains, we conduct ablations on the content of the supervision signal. First, replacing the rationale with a sparse, single-word dimension label severely degrades performance as shown in Table 10. Second, fine-tuning on choice-only and generic CoT rationales fails to match the performance of our dimension-grounded rationales in Table 11, confirming that the gains stem specifically from the injection of human cognitive priors rather than task-specific fine-tuning.

H.6 Neuroscientific Analysis Details

Positive RSA shifts are observed across the ventral occipito-temporal cortex, encompassing category-selective regions such as the EBA, FFA, and PPA. This indicates that the aligned MLLMs representational geometry better captures the high-level semantic organization for object and category discrimination. Because these alignment gains are localized to high-level visual cortices, they reflect an abstraction of category- and shape-relevant semantic structures, rather than mere low-level retinotopic or pixel-wise feature matching.

Furthermore, we observe substantial alignment shifts extending into the IPS and RSC. Given the triplet comparison nature of the O1O task, the engagement of the IPS aligns with its established role in the dorsal attention and multiple-demand networks, facilitating top-down attentional selection and relational comparison. Concurrently, shifts within the RSC likely indicate enhanced alignment with memory-linked contextual and scene-associative representations. Taken together, these neural effects demonstrate that our framework drives the MLLMs to capture behaviorally relevant, higher-order similarity structures. Beyond behavioral task performance, these results provide a convergent, neural-level validation: anchoring MLLMs to behavior-derived semantic dimensions explicitly steers their internal representations toward human-like cognitive geometry.

H.7 Similarity of Behavioral Representational Geometry Details

To assess whether the global decision-making structure of the models aligns with human cognition, we perform RSA based on the behavioral choices in the O1O task. This section details the construction of the choice-based RSMs and the subsequent calculation of the geometry similarity scores.

Choice-based RSM.

We evaluate the representational geometry on a subset of N=48N=48 objects, yielding an N×NN\times N matrix for human and evaluating models (Baseline, CogAlign, and Centaur). We initialize an all-zero similarity matrix S∈ℝN×NS\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}.

The evaluation dataset consists of approximately 91.56K triplets drawn from this 48-object subset. For each triplet iteration t={oi,oj,ok}t=\{o_{i},o_{j},o_{k}\}, the models are tasked with selecting the odd-one-out object using CoT. Let the chosen odd-one-out be ok∈to_{k}\in t. The remaining two objects, denoted as (oi,oj)(o_{i},o_{j}), are deemed the most similar pair within the context of this triplet. We then update the similarity matrix by incrementing the co-occurrence counts for this pair (i,j)(i,j) and (j,i)(j,i):

Si,j←Si,j+1andSj,i←Sj,i+1S_{i,j}\leftarrow S_{i,j}+1\quad\text{and}\quad S_{j,i}\leftarrow S_{j,i}+1

This process is repeated across all triplets in the subset. The resulting matrix SS captures the global behavioral representational geometry of the models. Using this method, we derive the human RSM (ShumanS_{\text{human}}) and model RSM (SmodelS_{\text{model}}).

Quantifying representational geometry similarity.

We extract the upper triangular portion of their respective symmetric matrices, excluding the main diagonal. Let 𝐯human∈ℝD\mathbf{v}_{\text{human}}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and 𝐯model∈ℝD\mathbf{v}_{\text{model}}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} be the flattened 1D vectors derived from the upper triangles of ShumanS_{\text{human}} and SmodelS_{\text{model}} respectively, where D=N⁡(N−1)/2D=N(N-1)/2. The behavioral representational geometry similarity is quantified using the Pearson correlation:

Similarity Score=ρ⁡(𝐯model,𝐯human)\text{Similarity Score}=\rho(\mathbf{v}_{\text{model}},\mathbf{v}_{\text{human}}) (14)

where ρ⁡(⋅,⋅)\rho(\cdot,\cdot) is the Pearson correlation coefficient across the DD feature dimensions.

Appendix K Impact Statement

This work presents research on aligning Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with latent structure of human cognition. The primary positive impact is advancing our understanding of MLLMs by thinking process before decision-making, providing a data-driven framework to bridge the representational gap between models and human similarity judgements, making MLLMs more human-like. However, because our framework relies on crowdsourced behavioral data provided by Hebart et al., it carries the inherent risk of internalizing and transferring implicit human cognitive biases or stereotypes present in the dataset. To mitigate this, we advise future research to audit behavior-derived datasets for cultural and demographic biases prior to alignment.

Appendix L Dataset Licenses

We use the M4-Instruct dataset (Li et al., 2025), THINGS behavioral dataset (Hebart et al., 2020; Hebart et al., 2023), and Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) (Allen et al., 2022) following their respective license agreements. Both datasets are accessed through their official releases and use exclusively for academic research purposes.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  56. 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  57. Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  58. Answer: [Yes]

  59. Justification: We have cited all necessary papers and the license information and usage details of the datasets are provided in Appendix L.

  60. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.

    • •

      The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.

    • •

      The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.

    • •

      The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.

    • •

      For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.

    • •

      If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

    • •

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.

  61. 13.

    New assets

  62. Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?

  63. Answer: [Yes]

  64. Justification: The released code and related data are documented at https://github.com/ening-open/cogalign.

  65. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets.

    • •

      Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc.

    • •

      The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used.

    • •

      At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.

  66. 14.

    Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects

  67. Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?

  68. Answer: [N/A]

  69. Justification: This work does not involve crowdsourcing experiments or research with human subjects.

  70. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.

    • •

      According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector.

  71. 15.

    Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects

  72. Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained?

  73. Answer: [N/A]

  74. Justification: [N/A]

  75. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.

    • •

      We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution.

    • •

      For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review.

  76. 16.

    Declaration of LLM usage

  77. Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required.

  78. Answer: [Yes]

  80. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components.
